research.query: What extinguishes a fire in microgravity?
research.answer:
The question was matched to: extinction, microgravity. Below is what the indexed documents state about it, quoted with their sources.

**Evidence**
- ACME/Flame Design: 2. Microgravity spherical diffusion flames extinguish when the peak temperature first decreases below 1130 K. [S1]
- Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames: 3) Verify the phenomena observed on the ISS flame extinguishment experiments. [S2]
- ACME BRE: BRE yielded important data relevant to spacecraft fire safety. Quasi-steady burning corresponding to various condensed-phase materials (such as PMMA and Nylon) was observed in microgravity despite the absence of air flow, where the cessation of ventilation is an established… [S3]
- BASS: BASS Burning and Suppression of Solids. Spacecraft Fire Safety. Microgravity Science Glovebox [S4]
- FLEX-2: FLEX-2 Flame Extinguishment Experiment - 2. Spacecraft Fire Safety. Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), Multi-user Droplet Combustion Appartatus (MDCA) [S5]
- Dust can look like smoke to a particle counter: DAFT showed that a modified commercial particle counter could be used in microgravity, measuring a test dust aerosol released on the ISS. Limitation: Terrestrial test dust, not lunar regolith; feasibility test only. [S10]
- BASS-II maps solid-fuel burning down to 13.6 % O2: BASS-II ran 129 tests with initial O2 between 13.6 and 22.2 % vol, mostly on PMMA, SIBAL (cotton-fiberglass fabric), Nomex. Flow annotations record extinction in 15 tests, blow-off in 3 and no ignition in 1. Limitation: Outcome annotations  [S11]

**Limits**
- Extractive answer (no language model configured): passages are quoted, not interpreted.
- Only documents in this knowledge base were searched.

sources.title: ACME BRE — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator — researchImpacts
sources.text: BRE yielded important data relevant to spacecraft fire safety. Quasi-steady burning corresponding to various condensed-phase materials (such as PMMA and Nylon) was observed in microgravity despite the absence of air flow, where the cessation of ventilation is an established step in putting out spacecraft fires. The ongoing combustion without air flow was notably seen in elevated-oxygen atmospheres which are being considered for use in future spacecraft, whereas such flames in a normal atmosphere of 21% oxygen self-extinguished in a short time.

sources.title: BASS — Burning and Suppression of Solids — summary
sources.text: Flame spread and extinction over realistic solid fuels (cotton-fiberglass fabric, PMMA in several geometries, Nomex) in low-speed forced flow aboard the ISS. Built to bridge the gap between the 1-g NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 screening method and real microgravity flammability, and to test an inert gaseous extinguishing agent.

sources.title: BASS-II maps solid-fuel burning down to 13.6 % O2
sources.text: BASS-II ran 129 tests with initial O2 between 13.6 and 22.2 % vol, mostly on PMMA, SIBAL (cotton-fiberglass fabric), Nomex. Flow annotations record extinction in 15 tests, blow-off in 3 and no ignition in 1. sources.title: Cool flames: combustion at 500–1000 K
sources.text: Cool diffusion flames have peak temperatures of about 500–1000 K. FLEX, CFI and CFI-G studied them on droplets and burners in microgravity. Limitation: Research fuels and configurations; relevance to cabin fires is an open question, not a finding.

sources.title: More oxygen: droplet flames more often survive to burnout
sources.text: FLEX droplet tests in N2-only atmospheres that ended in flame extinction before burnout — Heptane: 5/17 at 21 % O2 vs 0/11 at 30–34 % O2; Methanol: 9/12 at 21 % O2 vs 2/13 at 30–34 % O2. Remaining tests ended in burnout ('completion') or droplet disruption. Limitation: Isolated droplets, two fuels; 'extinction' here means the flame went out before the droplet was consumed (often radiative), not the action of an extinguisher. Counts, not a model.

top_passage.text: This investigation hypothesizes that due to large differences between fire behavior in normal and reduced gravity, the use of terrestrial fires and fire standards to design spacecraft fire safety systems presents an inherent risk to the vehicle because of the significant level of uncertainty. While this approach has been successful thus far, the uncertainty and risk will increase as exploration missions venture further from earth with considerably longer transit times for a safe return. There is a significant lack of microgravity data available for spacecraft designers on which to base their fire safety designs and procedures.

top_passage.text: The objective of this ground investigation was to use flight data obtained from PSI through NASA’s Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) to quantify how externally imposed thermal and convective perturbations regulated the dynamics and ultimate fate of already established droplet cool flames, and to explain run-to-run variability by isolating the roles of deliberate heating and unintentional drift-induced convection. Focusing on both small and large droplets, the work mapped stability windows for ignition, sustained oscillation, transitions to hot ignition and warm-flame behavior, and extinction under microgravity.
